item.title: “Monks, just as in the last month of the rainy season, in autumn, when the rice has ripened, a cowherd tending cows would poke the…
item.description:
“Monks, just as in the last month of the rainy season, in autumn, when the rice has ripened, a cowherd tending cows would poke the cows on this side and that with a stick, restraining and checking them. Why is that? Because the cowherd sees that otherwise there would be death, imprisonment, beating, or blame. Monks, even so, I saw the peril, the degradation, the defilement of unwholesome states, and I saw the escape, the benefit, the purification of wholesome states.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 19 – Dvedhāvitakkasutta

item.title: “Abandon desire, abandon greed — These are the bonds of worldlings. The one with eyes walks the path, Crosses hell and human birth. Eating little,…
item.description:
“Abandon desire, abandon greed —
These are the bonds of worldlings.
The one with eyes walks the path,
Crosses hell and human birth.

Eating little, moderate in food,
With few wishes, not greedy —
He is without desire, without craving,
Truly at peace.

Having gone on alms-round,
The sage enters the forest,
Goes to the root of a tree,
Prepares his sitting place.

The wise one, meditating,
Delights in the forest,
Meditating at the root of a tree,
Content, he practices his own pleasure.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 3.11

item.title: “Hearing the Buddha’s words, The wise monk fully understands the body, Sees it as it really is. As it is below, so above, As above,…
item.description:
“Hearing the Buddha’s words,
The wise monk fully understands the body,
Sees it as it really is.

As it is below, so above,
As above, so below —
Abandoning desire for the body inside and out,

The wise monk abandons desire and lust.
He attains the deathless, peace,
The constant state of Nibbāna.

This two-footed, impure, foul-smelling body
Filled with various rotting corpses, oozing —
Yet it is preserved and honored.

Who would think to exalt this body,
Or despise another —
Except one who is blind?”

From: Sutta Nipāta 1.11
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Hemavata: “Who here has crossed the flood? Who here has crossed the ocean? Without footing, without clinging — Who does not sink into the deep?”…
item.description:
Hemavata:
“Who here has crossed the flood?
Who here has crossed the ocean?
Without footing, without clinging —
Who does not sink into the deep?”

The Blessed One:
“One always virtuous, wise,
Well-concentrated, inwardly directed,
Mindful — crosses the flood so hard to cross.

One who has abandoned sense-desire perceptions,
Who has overcome all fetters,
Who has destroyed delight in existence —
Does not sink into the deep.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 1.9

item.title: Few among humans Reach the further shore, While the rest of humankind Run up and down on this shore. Those who practice the Dhamma In…
item.description:
Few among humans
Reach the further shore,
While the rest of humankind
Run up and down on this shore.
Those who practice the Dhamma
In accordance with the well-taught Dhamma,
Will reach the further shore,
Beyond the realm of death, so hard to escape.
The wise, having left the dark state,
Should develop the bright,
Leaving home for the homeless life,
Living in seclusion, where pleasure is hard to find.
Seeking delight in Nibbāna,
Having abandoned sensual pleasures, without possessions,
The wise should cleanse themselves
Of defilements of the mind.
Those who have well developed the factors of enlightenment
With a mind rightly directed,
Who, without clinging, delight in the abandoning of grasping —
They, the defilement-free, the radiant,
Attain final Nibbāna in the world.

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.117
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: - What gives birth to a person? What always runs about? What undergoes rebirth? What does a person rely on? - Craving gives birth to…
item.description:
- What gives birth to a person?
What always runs about?
What undergoes rebirth?
What does a person rely on?
- Craving gives birth to a person,
The mind itself always runs about,
Beings undergo rebirth,
Kamma is what a person relies on.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.57

item.title: “Brahmin, if an elder is eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, and he enjoys sensual pleasures, dwells amidst sensual pleasures, is burned by the…
item.description:
“Brahmin, if an elder is eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, and he enjoys sensual pleasures, dwells amidst sensual pleasures, is burned by the fever of sensual pleasures, consumed by sensual thoughts, and strives for sensual pleasures — such a person is called a fool, not an elder. But if a young person, brahmin, a youth with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, does not enjoy sensual pleasures, does not dwell amidst sensual pleasures, is not burned by the fever of sensual pleasures, not consumed by sensual thoughts, and does not strive for sensual pleasures — such a person is called a wise one, an elder.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.38

item.title: “Furthermore, monks, with sensuality as the cause, sensuality as the source, sensuality as the basis, simply because of sensuality, they engage in misconduct of body,…
item.description:
“Furthermore, monks, with sensuality as the cause, sensuality as the source, sensuality as the basis, simply because of sensuality, they engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, misconduct of mind. Having engaged in misconduct of body, speech, and mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a plane of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell. Monks, such is the peril of sensuality, leading to future suffering, a mass of suffering, with sensuality as the cause, sensuality as the source, sensuality as the basis – simply because of sensuality.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 13 – Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta

item.title: “Nāgita, for those who are heavily inclined toward delight, when there is change, alteration, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise — that is the…
item.description:
“Nāgita, for those who are heavily inclined toward delight, when there is change, alteration, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise — that is the natural result. For those who fix their minds on the sign of the foul, Nāgita, disenchantment with the sign of the beautiful becomes established — that is the natural result. For one who dwells contemplating impermanence in the six sense bases, Nāgita, disenchantment with contact becomes established — that is the natural result. For one who dwells contemplating arising and passing away in the five aggregates of clinging, Nāgita, disenchantment with clinging becomes established — that is the natural result.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.30

item.title: “I do not see any other thing, monks, through which unarisen factors of enlightenment arise and arisen factors of enlightenment come to completion, as wise…
item.description:
“I do not see any other thing, monks, through which unarisen factors of enlightenment arise and arisen factors of enlightenment come to completion, as wise attention. Through wise attention, monks, unarisen factors of enlightenment arise and arisen factors of enlightenment come to full development.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.75
